summary: magnification (M) is what the Telescope magnification calculator works out, and it gets there from the objective focal point, the eyepiece field of view and the resolving power. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Telescope magnification calculator work?
sections.html:
The Telescope magnification calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports magnification (M) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the objective focal point (fₒ), the eyepiece field of view (FOVₑ) and the resolving power (Pᵣ).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Telescope magnification calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Magnification (M)=objective focal point (fₒ) ÷ eyepiece focal length (fₑ)
Objective's diameter (Dₒ)=(579 ÷ 5) ÷ resolving power (Pᵣ)
Magnification (M)=eyepiece field of view (FOVₑ) ÷ scope field of view (FOVₛ)
Objective's diameter (Dₒ)=objective focal point (fₒ) ÷ f-ratio (fᵣ)
Star magnitude limit (Lₘ)=5 × (objective's diameter (Dₒ)) + 2
F-ratio (fᵣ)=eyepiece focal length (fₑ) ÷ exit pupil diameter (Dₑₚ)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Eyepiece focal length (fₑ) = 30 mm, Objective focal point (fₒ) = 30 mm and Eyepiece field of view (FOVₑ) = 52 deg. Working through the relationship above gives Magnification (M) = 1 and Scope field of view (FOVₛ) = 52 deg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Magnification (M) = 1 and Scope field of view (FOVₛ) = 52 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Eyepiece focal length (fₑ) = 30 mm and Objective focal point (fₒ) = 30 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Angle, opening in seconds of arc
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Telescope magnification calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the objective focal point, the eyepiece field of view and the resolving power — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Telescope magnification calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns magnification (M), derived from the objective focal point, the eyepiece field of view and the resolving power. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Telescope magnification calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the objective focal point, the eyepiece field of view and the resolving power, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter objective's diameter (Dₒ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Objective's diameter (Dₒ) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Magnification (M) = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Telescope magnification calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
